lessons.title: 1.2 Reading - Stop Telling Lies: The Story and Its Characters
lessons.notes_html:
The Story

Memna is a little baby goat. She likes to go to the pond every day to drink water and play there. At the pond she meets Jabir, the big bad wolf. Jabir tells lies. He says the pond is his alone and he wants to eat Memna. Memna is small but brave and clever. She does not believe the wolf's lies and calls her friends for help.

The Characters

  • Jabir - the big bad wolf. He tells lies and tries to frighten the small animals. In the end he is taught a lesson and runs away.
  • Memna - the baby goat. She is small, brave and clever.
  • Mano - a fluffy black cat. She is kind and quick to help. She says, "Don't worry."
  • Moti - a fat brown dog. He is strong and friendly. He says, "Don't be upset, I'll help you."
  • Kumet - a big red horse. He is gentle and caring. He says, "Don't cry."

Who Said These Words?

  • "Don't be upset, I'll help you." - Moti the dog said this.
  • "Don't cry!" - Kumet the horse said this.
  • "Don't worry!" - Mano the cat said this.
  • "The big bad wolf is coming to eat me!" - Memna said this.
  • "I've come to eat you." - Jabir the wolf said this.

Questions and Answers

  • Memna likes to go to the pond every day.
  • At the pond, Memna meets Jabir, the big bad wolf.
  • In the end, her friends Mano, Moti and Kumet help her, and together they teach the wolf a lesson.

Key Points

  • Memna is a baby goat who goes to the pond every day.
  • Jabir is a big bad wolf who tells lies.
  • Memna's friends help her and teach the wolf a lesson.

mcqs.q: Who is Memna?
mcqs.why: Memna is a little baby goat. She is small and sweet, and she likes to play near the pond.

mcqs.q: Who is Jabir?
mcqs.why: Jabir is the big bad wolf. He tells lies and wants to eat Memna at the pond.

mcqs.q: Where does Memna like to go every day?
mcqs.why: Memna likes to go to the pond every day to drink water and play there.

mcqs.q: Whom does Memna meet at the pond?
mcqs.why: At the pond Memna meets Jabir, the big bad wolf, who tells lies and wants to eat her.

mcqs.q: Who said, "Don't worry!"?
mcqs.why: Mano the cat said, "Don't worry!" She is kind and quick to help Memna.

mcqs.q: Who said, "I've come to eat you."?
mcqs.why: Jabir the wolf said, "I've come to eat you." He wanted to eat Memna at the pond.

mcqs.q: Who said, "Don't cry!"?
mcqs.why: Kumet the horse said, "Don't cry!" Kumet is a big red horse who is gentle and caring.

mcqs.q: Who helps Memna in the end?
options: Her friends Mano, Moti and Kumet
mcqs.why: In the end her friends Mano the cat, Moti the dog and Kumet the horse help her, and together they teach the wolf a lesson.

mcqs.q: What kind of animal is Moti?
mcqs.why: Moti is a fat brown dog. He is strong and friendly, and he says, "Don't be upset, I'll help you."

mcqs.q: What happens to Jabir in the end?
options: He becomes Memna's friend at once
He is taught a lesson and runs away
He drinks all the pond water
mcqs.why: In the end Jabir is taught a lesson by Memna and her friends, and he runs away.

lessons.title: 1.2 Reading - Describing Words and Pronouns in the Story
lessons.notes_html:
Describing Words

Describing words tell us how the animals look in the picture.

  • Mano is a fluffy black cat.
  • Kumet is a big red horse.
  • Jabir is a big bad wolf.
  • Moti is a fat brown dog.

Pronouns

A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun. In the story:

  • my in "This is my pond" refers to Jabir. Jabir wrongly claims the pond is his alone.
  • I in "No, it's everybody's pond" refers to Memna, who bravely answers the wolf.
  • he in "On his way, he saw a cat" refers to Jabir, who met Mano the cat on his way.
  • it in "It's just over there" refers to the pond.
  • you in "I've come to eat you" refers to Memna, whom the wolf wants to eat.

Key Points

  • Fluffy, big, bad, fat and red are describing words.
  • A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun.
  • The pronoun 'it' refers to the pond in the story.

mcqs.q: Mano is a ______ black cat.
mcqs.why: Mano is a fluffy black cat. 'Fluffy' is the describing word used for Mano in the story picture.

mcqs.q: Kumet is a ______ horse.
mcqs.why: Kumet is a big red horse. The describing words 'big' and 'red' tell us how Kumet looks.

mcqs.q: The pronoun 'my' in "This is my pond" refers to:
mcqs.why: 'My' refers to Jabir the wolf, who wrongly claims that the pond is his alone.

mcqs.q: The pronoun 'I' in "No, it's everybody's pond" refers to:
mcqs.why: 'I' refers to Memna, who bravely answers the wolf that the pond is everybody's pond.

mcqs.q: The pronoun 'he' in "On his way, he saw a cat" refers to:
mcqs.why: 'He' refers to Jabir, who met Mano the cat on his way to the pond.

mcqs.q: The pronoun 'it' in "It's just over there" refers to:
mcqs.why: 'It' refers to the pond, which is near the place where they are standing.

mcqs.q: The pronoun 'you' in "I've come to eat you" refers to:
mcqs.why: 'You' refers to Memna, the baby goat whom the wolf wants to eat.

mcqs.q: Which word describes Moti?
mcqs.why: Moti is a fat brown dog, so 'fat' is the describing word for Moti. 'Fluffy' describes Mano and 'red' describes Kumet.

mcqs.q: A pronoun is a word that:
options: is used in place of a noun
mcqs.why: A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun, like he, she, it, my and you in the story.

mcqs.q: Jabir wrongly claims that the pond is:
mcqs.why: Jabir says, "This is my pond." He wrongly claims the pond is his alone, but Memna answers that it is everybody's pond.

lessons.title: 1.3 Writing - Adjectives: Describing Words
lessons.notes_html:
What Is an Adjective?

An adjective is a word that describes a noun. For example, a deep pond and a small goat.

Pick the Adjective

  • river, pond, deep, fish
  • small, cow, goat, donkey
  • grass, tree, tasty, fresh (fresh is also an adjective)
  • baby, cry, happy, doctor
  • fat, hut, sing, friend
  • house, lovely, car, pencil

Adjectives in Sentences

  • The white goat is drinking water.
  • The fresh grass is sweet for the goat.
  • The long river has fresh water.
  • It is as white as snow.
  • The kite is flying in the blue sky.

Adjectives for Nouns

  • Pomegranate: red, juicy, sweet
  • Elephant: big, grey, strong
  • Rainbow: colourful, bright, beautiful
  • Student: clever, hardworking, polite
  • Snake: long, thin, dangerous
  • Book: interesting, new, thick
  • Toy: small, lovely, plastic
  • Lion: brave, wild, strong

Adjectives in the Passage

In the passage about Memna and Jabir, the adjectives are: big (tree), naughty (mind), fresh (water) and suitable (reply).

Key Points

  • An adjective describes a noun.
  • Deep, small, tasty, happy, fat and lovely are adjectives.
  • Suitable adjectives make a sentence clear and interesting.

mcqs.q: Which word is an adjective: river, pond, deep, fish?
mcqs.why: 'Deep' is an adjective because it describes a noun, as in 'a deep pond'. River, pond and fish are nouns.

mcqs.q: Which set of adjectives fits an elephant?
mcqs.why: The book gives big, grey and strong as adjectives for an elephant. Red, juicy and sweet describe a pomegranate.

mcqs.q: The ______ goat is drinking water.
mcqs.why: The book's answer is: 'The white goat is drinking water.' 'White' is the adjective that describes the goat.

mcqs.q: In the passage, the adjective used for 'tree' is:
mcqs.why: The passage says Jabir was standing under a big tree, so 'big' describes the tree. 'Naughty' describes his mind.

mcqs.q: In the passage, 'naughty' describes Jabir's:
mcqs.why: The passage says, 'Having a naughty mind, Jabir asks Memna...' So 'naughty' describes Jabir's mind.

mcqs.q: Which word is an adjective: house, lovely, car, pencil?
mcqs.why: 'Lovely' is an adjective because it describes a noun. House, car and pencil are nouns.

mcqs.q: Which adjectives describe a snake in the book?
mcqs.why: The book gives long, thin and dangerous for a snake. Brave, wild and strong are given for a lion.

mcqs.q: It is as ______ as snow.
mcqs.why: The book's sentence is: 'It is as white as snow.' 'White' is the adjective that matches the colour of snow.

mcqs.q: An adjective is a word that describes a:
mcqs.why: An adjective is a word that describes a noun, for example a deep pond and a small goat.

mcqs.q: Which pair of adjectives fits a rainbow?
mcqs.why: The book gives colourful, bright and beautiful as adjectives for a rainbow.

lessons.title: 1.3 Writing - Describing a Cat and Writing Your Own Sentences
lessons.notes_html:
About This Lesson

This is a writing practice lesson. There are no fixed answers. The book gives model answers to learn from.

Describing a Cat

Mano is a fluffy black cat. She has soft fur, sharp eyes and a long tail, and she runs very fast. The adjectives fluffy, black, soft and long tell us how the cat looks and feels.

Writing Sentences of Your Own

Choose one topic: A day in the park, A day in the zoo, or The best day of my life.

Model answer - The best day of my life: The best day of my life was the day our class went on a picnic. We played games, ate tasty food and laughed a lot with our friends. I can never forget that happy day.

Key Points

  • Use adjectives to describe how a person or animal looks and feels.
  • Mano has soft fur, sharp eyes and a long tail.
  • In the model answer, the best day was the class picnic day.

mcqs.q: In the model answer, Mano is a ______ cat.
mcqs.why: The model answer begins: 'Mano is a fluffy black cat.' Fluffy and black describe how the cat looks.

mcqs.q: The cat in the model answer has ______ fur.
mcqs.why: The model answer says: 'She has soft fur, sharp eyes and a long tail.' So her fur is soft.

mcqs.q: The cat has a ______ tail.
mcqs.why: The model answer says the cat has a long tail. 'Long' is an adjective describing the tail.

mcqs.q: Which one is a writing topic in this lesson?
options: The best day of my life
mcqs.why: The three topics are: A day in the park, A day in the zoo, and The best day of my life.

mcqs.q: In the model answer, the best day was the day of the class:
mcqs.why: The model answer says: 'The best day of my life was the day our class went on a picnic.'

mcqs.q: What did they eat at the picnic in the model answer?
mcqs.why: The model answer says: 'We played games, ate tasty food and laughed a lot with our friends.'

mcqs.q: Which adjective describes the day in the model answer?
mcqs.why: The model answer ends: 'I can never forget that happy day.' So 'happy' describes the day.

mcqs.q: The cat in the model answer runs very:
mcqs.why: The model answer says the cat 'runs very fast'. This tells us how the cat moves.

mcqs.q: Which adjective tells how the cat's eyes are?
mcqs.why: The model answer says the cat has 'sharp eyes', so 'sharp' describes her eyes. 'Soft' describes her fur.

mcqs.q: "I can never forget that ______ day."
mcqs.why: The model answer ends with these words: 'I can never forget that happy day.'

lessons.title: 1.4 Grammar - Present Continuous Tense
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

In the present continuous tense we use is / are / am with the verb + ing to show an action happening now. Remember: I takes 'am', he / she / it takes 'is', and you / we / they take 'are'.

Changed Sentences

  • I buy new books. - I am buying new books.
  • They plant the trees. - They are planting the trees.
  • It rains heavily today. - It is raining heavily today.
  • The teacher teaches English in our class. - The teacher is teaching English in our class.

Make Sentences

  • I am eating my lunch.
  • He is reading a story book.
  • She is going to school.
  • You are running in the ground.
  • We are singing a song.
  • They are eating mangoes.

Correct the Sentences

  • She is writing a letter. (not 'wrtting')
  • The doctor is examining the patient.
  • It is raining. (not 'are')
  • I am reading a book. (not 'is')
  • The cat is running after the mouse. (not 'are')

Key Points

  • Present continuous = am / is / are + verb-ing.
  • The helping verb must agree with the subject.
  • The main verb always takes -ing in this tense.

mcqs.q: Change into present continuous: "They plant the trees."
options: They plant the trees now yesterday.
mcqs.why: 'They' takes 'are', and the verb takes -ing: 'They are planting the trees.'

mcqs.q: I ______ reading a book.
mcqs.why: With 'I' we always use 'am': 'I am reading a book.' The book's sentence 'I is reading' is wrong.

mcqs.q: The cat ______ running after the mouse.
mcqs.why: 'The cat' is one animal (it), so we use 'is': 'The cat is running after the mouse.'

mcqs.q: Which sentence is correct?
mcqs.why: 'She is writing a letter' is correct. The spelling is 'writing', 'she' takes 'is', and the verb takes -ing.

mcqs.q: The doctor is ______ the patient.
mcqs.why: In the present continuous tense the main verb takes -ing: 'The doctor is examining the patient.'

mcqs.q: He is ______ a story book.
mcqs.why: 'He is reading a story book' is the present continuous form: is + verb-ing.

mcqs.q: We ______ singing a song.
mcqs.why: With 'we' we use 'are': 'We are singing a song.'

mcqs.q: Change into present continuous: "It rains heavily today."
mcqs.why: 'It' takes 'is' and 'rain' takes -ing: 'It is raining heavily today.'

mcqs.q: In the present continuous tense, the main verb takes:
mcqs.why: We use is / are / am with the verb + ing to show an action happening now, like buying, planting and teaching.

mcqs.q: "He is happy to see his friend" in the present continuous is best written as:
options: He is being happy to see his friend.
He is feeling happy to see his friend.
He are happy to see his friend.
He is happying to see his friend.
mcqs.why: The book prints 'is being happy', but we do not use 'being' with 'happy'. 'He is feeling happy to see his friend' is the correct continuous form, as the book's own note also gives.

lessons.title: 1.4 Grammar - What Is Everyone Doing?
lessons.notes_html:
Animals and Their Names

The pictures are matched with these names: camel, peacock, monkey, parrot, elephant, pigeon, hen, peahen. A peacock is the male bird with long colourful feathers, and a peahen is the female bird.

What Is Everyone Doing?

  • Nazo is sleeping.
  • Fahim is swimming.
  • Farhan is reading a book.
  • Bachal is eating apples.
  • Rabia is writing.
  • Natasha is drinking.
  • Imran is playing football.
  • Najma is skipping. (given in the book as the example)

All these sentences are in the present continuous tense.

Key Points

  • A peacock is the male bird; a peahen is the female.
  • 'Is + verb-ing' tells what a person is doing now.
  • Najma is skipping - this is the book's example sentence.

mcqs.q: Who is sleeping?
mcqs.why: In the book's matching, Nazo is sleeping. Fahim is swimming and Imran is playing football.

mcqs.q: Fahim is:
mcqs.why: Fahim is swimming. All the sentences in this exercise are in the present continuous tense.

mcqs.q: Who is reading a book?
mcqs.why: Farhan is reading a book. Bachal is eating apples and Natasha is drinking.

mcqs.q: Bachal is eating:
mcqs.why: Bachal is eating apples, as matched in the book's exercise.

mcqs.q: Who is playing football?
mcqs.why: Imran is playing football. Fahim is swimming and Farhan is reading a book.

mcqs.q: Najma is:
mcqs.why: Najma is skipping. This sentence is given in the book as the example.

mcqs.q: A peahen is:
options: the male bird with long colourful feathers
mcqs.why: A peahen is the female bird. The peacock is the male bird with long colourful feathers.

mcqs.q: Rabia is:
mcqs.why: Rabia is writing, as matched in the book's exercise. Natasha is drinking.

mcqs.why: Natasha is drinking. Rabia is writing and Nazo is sleeping.

mcqs.why: Sentences like 'Nazo is sleeping' and 'Imran is playing football' use is/are + verb-ing, which is the present continuous tense.

lessons.title: 1.4 Grammar - Short Forms (Contractions)
lessons.notes_html:
What Are Short Forms?

Short forms join two words into one word. For example: I have = I've, we are = we're, she is = she's, it will = it'll, I will = I'll, he will = he'll, you are = you're and do not = don't.

The Dialogue of Saeed and David

  • Saeed: I'll be going there tomorrow. I've asked my mother to do so.
  • She's also going. In fact, we're all going.
  • The goat: It'll be kept in my uncle's yard.
  • I don't know. I'll probably come back on the first, but my brother says he'll come back earlier.
  • David: You're so lucky. I'll go to Sialkot with my family.

Key Points

  • Short forms join two words into one.
  • I've = I have, we're = we are, it'll = it will.
  • David will go to Sialkot with his family.

mcqs.q: "I've" is the short form of:
mcqs.why: I've is the short form of 'I have'. In the dialogue Saeed says, "I've asked my mother to do so."

mcqs.q: "We're" is the short form of:
mcqs.why: We're joins 'we are' into one word: "In fact, we're all going."

mcqs.q: Complete the dialogue: "______ asked my mother to do so."
mcqs.why: Saeed says, "I've asked my mother to do so." I've is the short form of 'I have'.

mcqs.q: The goat: "______ be kept in my uncle's yard."
mcqs.why: "It'll be kept in my uncle's yard." It'll is the short form of 'it will'.
Saeed says, "I don't know." Don't is the short form of 'do not'.

mcqs.q: David says: "______ go to Sialkot with my family."
mcqs.why: David says, "I'll go to Sialkot with my family." I'll is the short form of 'I will'.

mcqs.q: In "She's also going", the short form 'she's' means:
mcqs.why: Here 'she's' means 'she is': "She's also going." She's joins 'she is' into one word.

mcqs.q: "He'll" is the short form of:
mcqs.why: He'll joins 'he will' into one word: "My brother says he'll come back earlier."

mcqs.q: "You're so lucky" - 'you're' means:
mcqs.why: You're is the short form of 'you are'. David says, "You're so lucky."

mcqs.q: Short forms join ______ words into one word.
mcqs.why: Short forms join two words into one, like I have = I've and we are = we're.

lessons.title: 1.5 Study Skills - Alphabetical Order and Making Words
lessons.notes_html:
Words Beginning with 'M'

The words beginning with 'M' in the story are: Memna, Mano, Moti, my and mine. Memna, Mano and Moti are the names of the animal characters. 'My' and 'mine' are pronoun words used in the dialogues.

Alphabetical Order

In alphabetical order the 'M' words are: Mano, Memna, mine, Moti, my. We look at the second letter of each word: 'a' (Mano) comes before 'e' (Memna), then 'i' (mine), then 'o' (Moti) and last 'y' (my).

Words from 'Goats'

Words that can be made from 'goats' are: go, got, goat, goats, gas, tag, sag, oat, sat, so, to, at, ago, stag, toast. Short words like go, at and to are hidden inside the big word.

In alphabetical order: ago, at, gas, go, goat, goats, got, oat, sag, sat, so, stag, tag, to.

Key Points

  • Alphabetical order is decided by the letters of the words.
  • Mano comes first and 'my' comes last among the 'M' words.
  • Many small words are hidden inside a big word like 'goats'.

mcqs.q: Which word from the story begins with the letter 'M'?
mcqs.why: Memna begins with 'M'. The 'M' words in the story are Memna, Mano, Moti, my and mine.

mcqs.q: In alphabetical order, which 'M' word comes first?
mcqs.why: Mano comes first because its second letter 'a' comes before 'e' in Memna, 'i' in mine and 'o' in Moti.

mcqs.q: In alphabetical order, which 'M' word comes last?
mcqs.why: The order is Mano, Memna, mine, Moti, my. The second letter 'y' in 'my' comes last.

mcqs.q: Which word can be made from the letters of 'goats'?
mcqs.why: 'Stag' uses only the letters of 'goats' (s, t, a, g). Dogs, fish and lamp need letters that are not in 'goats'.

mcqs.q: Which word can NOT be made from 'goats'?
mcqs.why: 'Boat' needs the letter 'b', which is not in 'goats'. Goat, gas and sat use only the letters of 'goats'.

mcqs.q: Which word comes first in alphabetical order among the words made from 'goats'?
mcqs.why: The alphabetical order begins: ago, at, gas, go... Words beginning with 'a' come first, so 'ago' is first.

mcqs.q: Which word comes last in alphabetical order among the words made from 'goats'?
mcqs.why: The order ends: ...stag, tag, to. Words beginning with 't' come last, and 'to' is the last word.

mcqs.q: Mano comes before Memna in alphabetical order because:
mcqs.why: When first letters are the same, we look at the second letter: 'a' (Mano) comes before 'e' (Memna).

mcqs.q: Which word made from 'goats' is the name of an animal?
mcqs.why: A stag is an animal (a male deer), and its letters s, t, a, g are all found in 'goats'.

mcqs.q: In alphabetical order, words beginning with 'a' come:
mcqs.why: Words beginning with 'a' come first, then 'g', then 'o', then 's' and last 't', as in the 'goats' word list.

lessons.title: 1.6 Fun - The Fun Twins: Tom and Jerry
lessons.notes_html:
About This Lesson

This is a fun activity lesson. The twins Tom and Jerry look alike and play tricks. We fill in the missing question or answer bubbles in their conversation.

The Missing Bubbles

  • Question: "Who took my socks?"
  • Answer: "I did not stuff your lunch box with rubber bands and rocks."
  • Question: "Who hid my sweater?"
  • Answer: "I did not dent your bike."

At the end the twin explains: "It must have been my sister. We look a lot alike." Because the twins look the same, people mix them up.

Key Points

  • Tom and Jerry are twins who look alike.
  • The lunch box was stuffed with rubber bands and rocks.
  • People mix up the twins because they look the same.

mcqs.q: The Fun Twins are named:
mcqs.why: The fun lesson is about the twins Tom and Jerry, who look alike and play tricks.

mcqs.q: Why do people mix up Tom and Jerry?
options: They have the same voice only
mcqs.why: Because the twins look the same, people mix them up. The twin says, "We look a lot alike."

mcqs.q: The missing question bubble is: "Who took my ______?"
mcqs.why: The missing question is: "Who took my socks?" It is one of the speech bubbles in the twins' conversation.

mcqs.q: The lunch box was stuffed with:
mcqs.why: The answer bubble says: "I did not stuff your lunch box with rubber bands and rocks."

mcqs.q: The second missing question is: "Who hid my ______?"
mcqs.why: The missing question is: "Who hid my sweater?" The answer to it is about the bike.

mcqs.q: "I did not dent your ______."
mcqs.why: The answer bubble says: "I did not dent your bike." To dent means to make a small hollow in something by hitting it.

mcqs.q: At the end, the twin says it must have been his:
mcqs.why: The twin explains: "It must have been my sister. We look a lot alike."

mcqs.q: "We look a lot ______."
mcqs.why: The twin says, "We look a lot alike." 'Alike' means the same in appearance.

mcqs.q: Tom and Jerry play:
mcqs.why: The twins look alike and play tricks, so people mix them up and blame the wrong twin.

mcqs.q: The answer bubble about the lunch box says the twin did NOT:
options: stuff the lunch box with rubber bands and rocks
mcqs.why: The bubble reads: "I did not stuff your lunch box with rubber bands and rocks." The twin denies doing it.

lessons.title: 2.2 Reading - The Pottery Making: Who Was Doing What?
lessons.notes_html:
The Text

One day Raja went to visit his aunt Sadori and uncle Jumman, who are potters. Raja is the narrator of the story. He saw how pots are made and learnt the work of each person.

Who Was Doing What?

  • Aunt Sadori was shaping a pot on a wheel. She was pushing the wheel with her hands to turn it.
  • Sara was making patterns on a bowl with a pointed bone.
  • Saleh was painting (colouring) a vase.
  • Alam, the hired boy, was coming with his donkey, carrying the clay from the river bank.
  • Raja went to visit his aunt and uncle.

Questions and Answers

  • When Raja got there, Aunt Sadori was shaping a pot on a wheel.
  • Raja learnt how pots are made: clay is mixed into a paste, pots are shaped on a wheel, dried in the sun, decorated with patterns, coloured and baked in a kiln.
  • The kiln is important because its heat bakes the soft clay pots and makes them hard and strong.

Key Points

  • Aunt Sadori shapes pots on a wheel.
  • Sara makes patterns and Saleh paints the vase.
  • The kiln makes the pots hard and strong.

mcqs.q: Who was shaping a pot on a wheel?
mcqs.why: Aunt Sadori was shaping a pot on a wheel, and she was pushing the wheel with her hands to turn it.

mcqs.q: Who was making patterns on a bowl?
mcqs.why: Sara was making patterns on a bowl with a pointed bone.

mcqs.q: Sara made patterns on the bowl with a:
mcqs.why: Sara drew patterns on a bowl with a pointed bone, as the pottery text tells us.

mcqs.q: Who was painting a vase?
mcqs.why: Saleh was painting (colouring) a vase. Aunt Sadori was shaping a pot on the wheel.

mcqs.q: Who was bringing clay on a donkey?
mcqs.why: Alam, the hired boy, was coming with his donkey carrying the clay from the river bank.

mcqs.q: Where did Raja go one day?
options: To his aunt and uncle's house
mcqs.why: One day Raja went to visit his aunt Sadori and uncle Jumman, who are potters.

mcqs.q: Aunt Sadori pushed the wheel with her:
mcqs.why: Aunt Sadori was pushing the wheel with her hands to turn it while she shaped the pot.

mcqs.q: The clay was brought from the:
mcqs.why: Alam was carrying the clay from the river bank on his donkey.

mcqs.q: Why is the kiln important?
options: Its heat bakes the pots and makes them hard and strong
It dries the pots in the sun
mcqs.why: The kiln is important because its heat bakes the soft clay pots and makes them hard and strong.

lessons.title: 2.2 Reading - How Pots Are Made: Steps, Tools and Pronouns
lessons.notes_html:
The Steps of Pottery Making

  • Saleh was making a paste from the clay.
  • Aunt Sadori shaped the pots on a wheel.
  • Sara put the pots out in the sun to dry.
  • She drew patterns on a bowl with a pointed bone.
  • Saleh coloured (painted) the vase.
  • Finally, Uncle Jumman put the pots in the kiln to bake.

What Is Needed for Each Job?

  • To bring clay - a donkey
  • To shape pots - a wheel
  • To draw patterns - a pointed bone
  • To colour vases - colours (paint)
  • To bake pots - a kiln

Pronouns in the Text

  • she (Aunt was shaping a pot... she was pushing the wheel) - Aunt Sadori
  • My (My cousin Sara) - Raja
  • She (Sara was sitting... she was drawing patterns) - Sara
  • I ("I'll come to your house") - Sara
  • you ("This will help you in your work") - Raja
  • It (the kiln: "It makes the pots hard") - the kiln
  • We ("We need more clay") - Uncle Jumman and his family, the potters
  • He (Alam... he was coming with his donkey) - Alam

Key Points

  • Pots are shaped on a wheel and baked in a kiln.
  • A pointed bone is used to draw patterns.
  • The pronoun 'It' refers to the kiln in the text.

lessons.title: 2.4 Grammar - Past Continuous Tense
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

In the past continuous tense we use was / were with the verb + ing. We use 'was' with I, he, she and it, and 'were' with you, we and they.

Changed Sentences

  • The boys were playing hockey.
  • The girls were singing a song.
  • The baby was crying loudly.
  • We were eating mangoes.
  • She was writing a letter.

Was or Were?

  • The farmer was sowing the seeds.
  • The children were playing in the field.
  • It was raining yesterday.
  • They were cutting the wheat.
  • I was watering the plants.

Saleem's Day

  • At 6:00 a.m. Saleem was washing his face. (given in the book as the example)
  • At 7:00 a.m. he was drinking tea.
  • At 8:00 a.m. he was reading a book.
  • At 9:00 a.m. he was polishing his shoes.
  • At 6:00 p.m. he was playing hockey.
  • At 7:00 p.m. he was watching TV.
  • At 8:00 p.m. he was writing a letter.
  • At 9:00 p.m. he was doing his homework.

Key Points

  • Past continuous = was / were + verb-ing.
  • 'Was' is used with I, he, she and it.
  • 'Were' is used with you, we and they.

mcqs.q: Change into past continuous: "The girls sing a song."
options: The girls was singing a song.
The girls were singing a song.
The girls are singing a song.
mcqs.why: 'The girls' is like 'they', so we use 'were': 'The girls were singing a song.'

mcqs.why: 'The farmer' is one person (he), so we use 'was': 'The farmer was sowing the seeds.'

mcqs.why: With 'I' we use 'was' in the past continuous: 'I was watering the plants.'

mcqs.why: In the past continuous tense we use was/were with the verb + ing, like 'was crying' and 'were eating'.

mcqs.q: At 6:00 p.m. Saleem was:
mcqs.why: At 6:00 p.m. Saleem was playing hockey. He watched TV at 7:00 p.m.

lessons.title: 2.4 Grammar - Asking Permission: May and Can
lessons.notes_html:
Asking Permission

We use may and can to ask for permission politely. 'May' is more polite and formal than 'can'.

Questions and Answers from the Pottery Text

  • "May I try to make a pot, Aunt Sadori?" - "No, you need a lot of practice before you can make a pot." (given in the book)
  • "Can I put these pots in the sun?" - "Yes, you can help your aunt by putting the pots in the sun."
  • "Can we play now, Sara?" - "No, we will play after I have made patterns on the bowl."
  • "Can I go with Uncle Jumman, Saleh?" - "Yes, please go with him. I'll finish painting this bowl, then I'll play with you."
  • "May I see what's inside the kiln?" - "Yes, but don't go too near because the kiln is very hot."
  • "Can I help you make the clay paste, Uncle Jumman?" - "Yes, you can help by putting water in the clay while I mix it."

Model Requests

  • "May I drink some water, please?"
  • "Can I open the window?"

Key Points

  • May and can are used to ask permission politely.
  • 'May' is more polite and formal than 'can'.
  • The kiln is very hot, so we must not go too near it.

lessons.title: 2.5 Study Skills - 'S' Words and Words from 'Country'
lessons.notes_html:
Words Beginning with 'S'

Words beginning with 'S' in the pottery text include: Sadori, Saleh, Sara, saw, said, shaping, she, sitting, smoke, some, standing and sun. In alphabetical order: Sadori, Saleh, Sara, said, saw, shaping, she, sitting, smoke, some, standing, sun.

Words from 'Country'

Words that can be made from 'Country' are: court, count, country, cry, cut, nut, out, our, run, rut, ton, tour, toy, try, turn, you, your, corn, cot, con, coy, nor, not, rot. Many small words are hidden in this one big word.

In alphabetical order: con, corn, cot, count, country, court, coy, cry, cut, nor, not, nut, our, out, rot, run, rut, ton, tour, toy, try, turn, you, your. First come the words beginning with 'c', then 'n', 'o', 'r', 't' and last 'y'.

Key Points

  • The pottery text has many words beginning with 'S'.
  • 'Con' comes first and 'your' comes last in the 'Country' word list.
  • Many small words are hidden in one big word.

mcqs.q: Which word beginning with 'S' is found in the pottery text?
mcqs.why: 'Smoke' is one of the 'S' words in the pottery text, along with Sadori, Saleh, Sara, said, saw, shaping and sun.

mcqs.why: 'Cart' needs the letter 'a', which is not in 'Country'. Corn, tour and nut use only Country's letters.

mcqs.q: Which word comes first in alphabetical order among the words made from 'Country'?

mcqs.q: Which word comes last in alphabetical order among the words made from 'Country'?

mcqs.q: Which word made from 'Country' means a journey?
mcqs.why: A 'tour' is a journey, and its letters t, o, u, r are all found in 'Country'.

mcqs.q: In alphabetical order, which word comes just after 'cot'?
mcqs.why: The order is: con, corn, cot, count, country, court. So 'count' comes just after 'cot'.

mcqs.q: Which word made from 'Country' is the name of a food grain?
mcqs.why: Corn is a food grain, and its letters c, o, r, n are all found in the word 'Country'.

lessons.title: 3.2 Reading - The Story of Zahra: People, Places and Word Meanings
lessons.notes_html:
People and Places in the Story

The people mentioned in "The Story of Zahra" are: Zahra, Mateen (her brother), Hazrat Rufaida and Florence Nightingale (the two famous nurses), Zahra's mother and father, her teacher and the headmaster.

The places mentioned are: her small village near Mirpur Sakro, her primary school and the Boys' Middle School in the nearby village.

Names of people and places always begin with a capital letter.

Word Meanings

  • true means real - this is the real story of Zahra, not an imaginary one.
  • worked means studied - Zahra worked hard at her lessons.
  • All right means okay - the headmaster agreed to take Zahra in his school.
  • cross means go through (pass by) - the villagers did not want Zahra to pass through their streets.
  • route means way - Zahra and Mateen had to take a longer way to school.
  • alone means without friends. (given in the book as the example)

Key Points

  • Zahra's brother is Mateen.
  • Hazrat Rufaida and Florence Nightingale were famous nurses.
  • 'Route' means way, and 'cross' means go through.

lessons.title: 3.4 Grammar - Comparing Things: -er than
lessons.notes_html:
The Comparative Degree

When we compare two things, we use the comparative degree of adjectives: adjective + -er + than.

Comparing Carts, Buses and Cars

  • A camel cart is bigger than a donkey cart.
  • A camel cart moves slower than a donkey cart.
  • A car is smaller than a bus.
  • A car moves faster than a bus.
  • A bicycle is cheaper than a car.

Comparing Famous Places and Rivers

  • Mount Everest is higher than K2.
  • The River Indus is shorter than the River Nile.
  • The Indian Ocean is smaller than the Atlantic Ocean.
  • The River Nile is longer than the River Indus.
  • K2 is lower than Mount Everest.

Key Points

  • Comparative degree = adjective + -er + than.
  • Bigger, slower, smaller, faster and cheaper are comparative forms.
  • Mount Everest is higher than K2.

mcqs.q: A camel cart is ______ than a donkey cart.
mcqs.why: The book's answer is: 'A camel cart is bigger than a donkey cart.' 'Bigger' is the comparative of big.

mcqs.q: A car moves ______ than a bus.
mcqs.why: The book's answer is: 'A car moves faster than a bus.' A car is smaller than a bus but moves faster.

mcqs.q: Mount Everest is ______ than K2.
mcqs.why: Mount Everest is higher than K2. K2 is lower than Mount Everest.

mcqs.q: The River Nile is ______ than the River Indus.
mcqs.why: The River Nile is longer than the River Indus. The Indus is shorter than the Nile.

mcqs.q: The Indian Ocean is ______ than the Atlantic Ocean.
mcqs.why: The Indian Ocean is smaller than the Atlantic Ocean. The Atlantic is larger than the Indian Ocean.

mcqs.q: A bicycle is ______ than a car.
mcqs.why: The book's answer is: 'A bicycle is cheaper than a car.' 'Cheaper' is the comparative of cheap.

mcqs.q: The words bigger, slower and faster are in the ______ degree.
mcqs.why: These adjectives are in the comparative degree, used with 'than' to compare two things.

mcqs.q: Which sentence is correct?
options: K2 is higher than Mount Everest.
K2 is lower than Mount Everest.
K2 is the higher than Everest.
K2 is more high than Everest.
mcqs.why: Mount Everest is higher than K2, so K2 is lower than Mount Everest.

mcqs.q: A camel cart moves ______ than a donkey cart.
mcqs.why: The book's answer is: 'A camel cart moves slower than a donkey cart.'

mcqs.q: To compare two things, we often add ______ to the adjective and use 'than'.
mcqs.why: We use the 'er' + than form: higher than, longer than, smaller than, as in this lesson's exercises.

lessons.title: 3.4 Grammar - Making Questions and Giving Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Making Questions

Rearrange the words to form correct questions. They all end with a question mark (?).

  • your mother going where is - Where is your mother going?
  • the little girl is what eating - What is the little girl eating?
  • book this why you are reading - Why are you reading this book?
  • my house are you when coming to - When are you coming to my house?
  • brother your is why crying - Why is your brother crying?
  • can you get how good marks - How can you get good marks?
  • your grandmother does live where - Where does your grandmother live?
  • favourite colour is what your - What is your favourite colour?
  • sad is why the little girl - Why is the little girl sad?
  • today is your mother how feeling - How is your mother feeling today?

Short Answers

In short answers, the question words (where, what, why...) are dropped and the main words of the question are used. Examples: My mother is going to the market. I can get good marks by studying hard. My favourite colour is green.

Key Points

  • A question begins with a question word and ends with a question mark.
  • Short answers drop the question word.
  • 'What is your favourite colour?' - 'My favourite colour is green.'

mcqs.q: Rearrange: "your mother going where is"
mcqs.why: The correct question is: 'Where is your mother going?' A question begins with the question word.

mcqs.q: Rearrange: "book this why you are reading"
options: Why you are reading this book?
Why are you reading this book?
This book why are you reading?
Are you reading why this book?
mcqs.why: The correct question is: 'Why are you reading this book?'

mcqs.q: Rearrange: "favourite colour is what your"
mcqs.why: The correct question is: 'What is your favourite colour?' The model answer is: 'My favourite colour is green.'

mcqs.q: Rearrange: "sad is why the little girl"
options: The little girl is why sad?
Why sad is the little girl?
Is the little girl why sad?
Why is the little girl sad?
mcqs.why: The correct question is: 'Why is the little girl sad?' The model answer says she is sad because her doll is broken.

mcqs.q: Every question ends with a:
mcqs.why: All the rearranged sentences are questions, and they all end with a question mark (?).

mcqs.q: Short answer to "Where is your mother going?"
options: My mother is going to the market.
mcqs.why: The model short answer is: 'My mother is going to the market.' The question word 'where' is dropped.

mcqs.q: Short answer to "How can you get good marks?"
options: I can get good marks by studying hard.
mcqs.why: The model answer is: 'I can get good marks by studying hard.'

mcqs.q: Short answer to "When are you coming to my house?"
options: I am coming to your house on Sunday.
mcqs.why: The model short answer is: 'I am coming to your house on Sunday.'

mcqs.q: Rearrange: "your grandmother does live where"
mcqs.why: The correct question is: 'Where does your grandmother live?' The model answer is: 'My grandmother lives in our village.'

mcqs.q: In short answers, which words of the question are dropped?
mcqs.why: In the answers the question words (where, what, why...) are dropped and the main words of the question are used.

lessons.title: 3.4 Grammar - Articles: A and An
lessons.notes_html:
The Rule

We use 'an' before words that begin with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u), and 'a' before words that begin with a consonant sound.

The Market Passage

My mother bought a dress and a bag. My sister bought a book, an inkpot and an eraser. My brother wanted a bat, an umbrella, a hat and a shirt. My father bought an ice cream, a packet of biscuits, a cake and an egg. We bought a papaya, a melon and an orange for grandmother. We all returned home in a taxi. We paid a hundred rupees to the taxi driver.

Key Points

  • 'An' comes before a vowel sound: an inkpot, an egg, an orange.
  • 'A' comes before a consonant sound: a dress, a bat, a taxi.
  • We say 'a hundred' because 'hundred' begins with the consonant sound 'h'.

mcqs.q: ______ umbrella
mcqs.why: 'Umbrella' begins with the vowel sound 'u', so we use 'an': an umbrella.

mcqs.q: ______ inkpot
mcqs.why: 'Inkpot' begins with the vowel sound 'i', so we use 'an': an inkpot.

mcqs.q: ______ dress
mcqs.why: 'Dress' begins with the consonant sound 'd', so we use 'a': a dress.
'Egg' begins with the vowel sound 'e', so we use 'an': an egg.

mcqs.q: ______ taxi
mcqs.why: 'Taxi' begins with the consonant sound 't', so we use 'a': 'We all returned home in a taxi.'

mcqs.q: ______ hundred rupees
mcqs.why: We say 'a hundred rupees' because 'hundred' begins with the consonant sound 'h', not a vowel sound.

mcqs.q: We use 'an' before a word that begins with a:
mcqs.why: We use 'an' before words that begin with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u), like an eraser and an orange.

mcqs.q: ______ ice cream
mcqs.why: 'Ice cream' begins with the vowel sound 'i', so we use 'an': 'My father bought an ice cream.'

mcqs.q: ______ orange
mcqs.why: 'Orange' begins with the vowel sound 'o', so we use 'an': an orange for grandmother.
'Bat' begins with the consonant sound 'b', so we use 'a': 'My brother wanted a bat.'

lessons.title: 3.4 Grammar - The Article 'The' and Using A, An, The
lessons.notes_html:
When Do We Use 'The'?

We use 'the' with the sun, the sky, rivers, seas, directions and superlatives like 'the newest'.

Hamida and Rani's Dialogue

  • They have blocked the sun and the wind.
  • Look at the sky! The clouds are coming in very fast!
  • The rain is coming from the Arabian Sea.
  • The wind is blowing from the south.
  • Move the newest boat away from the River Indus.

The Pakistan Passage

  • Pakistan is a big country. It has the Arabian Sea in the south and high mountains in the north.
  • The longest river in Pakistan is the River Indus. It is a long river and falls into the Arabian Sea.
  • The highest peak in the world, Mount Everest, is in Nepal, but the second highest peak, K2, is in Pakistan.
  • We may see an ibex, a kind of mountain goat, or drink cold water from a stream, or see a hot water spring in Gilgit Baltistan.

Key Points

  • We say the sun, the sky, the River Indus and the Arabian Sea.
  • 'The' is used before superlatives like the longest and the newest.
  • The River Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.

mcqs.q: We say ______ sun.
mcqs.why: We use 'the' with the sun and the sky: 'They have blocked the sun and the wind.'

mcqs.q: The longest river in Pakistan is:
mcqs.why: The passage says: 'The longest river in Pakistan is the River Indus.' It travels from the north to the south.

mcqs.q: The second highest peak in the world, which is in Pakistan, is:
mcqs.why: The highest peak, Mount Everest, is in Nepal, but the second highest peak, K2, is in Pakistan.

mcqs.q: An ibex is a kind of:
mcqs.why: The passage says an ibex is a kind of mountain goat, which we may see in Gilgit Baltistan.

mcqs.q: Pakistan is ______ big country.
mcqs.why: The passage begins: 'Pakistan is a big country.' 'Big' begins with a consonant sound, so we use 'a'.

mcqs.q: The wind is blowing from ______ south.
mcqs.why: We use 'the' with directions: 'The wind is blowing from the south.'

mcqs.q: In 'the newest boat', we use 'the' because 'newest' is a:
mcqs.why: We use 'the' with superlatives like 'the newest', 'the longest' and 'the highest'.

mcqs.q: The River Indus falls into:
mcqs.why: The River Indus travels from the north of the country to the south, where it falls into the Arabian Sea.

mcqs.q: ______ hot water spring
mcqs.why: The passage says 'a hot water spring'. 'Hot' begins with the consonant sound 'h', so we use 'a'.

mcqs.q: The highest peak in the world is in:
mcqs.why: The passage says: 'The highest peak in the world, Mount Everest, is in Nepal.'

lessons.title: 3.5 Study Skills - Garden Words and Words from 'Elephant'
lessons.notes_html:
Things We See in a Garden

Things we see in a garden are: grass, trees, flowers, roses, butterflies, birds, bees, a swing, a slide, a bench, green plants and a gardener. Children play on the slide and the swing, and butterflies fly over the flowers.

In alphabetical order: bees, bench, birds, butterflies, flowers, gardener, grass, green plants, roses, slide, swing, trees. Alphabetical order helps us find words quickly in a dictionary.

Words from 'Elephant'

Words that can be made from 'Elephant' are: elephant, ant, hen, pen, ten, net, eat, ate, tea, pan, nap, tap, pat, pet, let, lane, plane, plant, planet, pale, peal, leap, heel, help, pant, neat, heat, lean, tale, late, peel, peep. The longest words are planet and elephant itself.

Key Points

  • 'Bees' comes first and 'trees' comes last in the garden word list.
  • 'Planet' is one of the longest words made from 'Elephant'.
  • Alphabetical order helps us use a dictionary quickly.

mcqs.q: Which garden word comes first in alphabetical order?
mcqs.why: The alphabetical order begins: bees, bench, birds, butterflies... 'Bees' comes first because 'ee' comes before 'en'.

mcqs.q: Which garden word comes last in alphabetical order?
mcqs.why: The order ends: ...roses, slide, swing, trees. 'Trees' begins with 't' and comes last.

mcqs.q: Which word can be made from the letters of 'Elephant'?
mcqs.why: 'Planet' uses only the letters of 'Elephant'. Tiger needs 'g', which is not in 'Elephant'.

mcqs.q: Which word can NOT be made from 'Elephant'?
mcqs.why: 'Tiger' needs the letter 'g', which is not in 'Elephant'. Plant, ant and plane use only Elephant's letters.

mcqs.q: The longest words made from 'Elephant' are planet and:
mcqs.why: The book says: 'The longest words are planet and elephant itself.'

mcqs.q: Children play on the slide and the:
mcqs.why: The model answer says: 'Children play on the slide and the swing, and butterflies fly over the flowers.'

mcqs.q: Butterflies fly over the:
mcqs.why: The model answer says butterflies fly over the flowers in the garden.

mcqs.q: In the model sentences, the plane flies:
mcqs.why: The model sentence is: 'The plane flies high in the sky.'

mcqs.q: Alphabetical order helps us find words quickly in a:
mcqs.why: Alphabetical order helps us find words quickly in a dictionary, as the book's answer explains.

mcqs.q: Which of these do we see in a garden?
mcqs.why: A gardener works in a garden. The garden list includes grass, trees, flowers, roses and a gardener.

lessons.title: 3.6 Fun - Poem: I Wish...
lessons.notes_html:
About This Lesson

This is a fun activity lesson. We recite the poem "I wish..." by Jack Prelutsky loudly with actions.

The Poem

In the poem, the boy is tired of being little and thin. He wishes he were of giant size, ten foot three, with whiskers on his chin, so that no one would dare to tease him or take away his toys.

Model Answer

I do not like being shy and speaking in a low voice. I want to become brave and speak clearly in class. If I change, I will take part in class activities and make more friends.

Key Points

  • The poem 'I wish...' is by Jack Prelutsky.
  • The boy wishes he were of giant size, ten foot three.
  • He wishes so that no one would tease him or take his toys.

mcqs.q: The poem "I wish..." is written by:
mcqs.why: The poem 'I wish...' is by Jack Prelutsky, as the book tells us in this fun lesson.

mcqs.q: The boy in the poem is tired of being:
mcqs.why: In the poem the boy is tired of being little and thin, so he wishes to be big.

mcqs.q: The boy wishes he were of ______ size.
mcqs.why: He wishes he were of giant size, ten foot three, with whiskers on his chin.

mcqs.q: The boy wishes to be ______ tall.
mcqs.why: He wishes he were ten foot three, which is very tall like a giant.

mcqs.q: The boy wishes for ______ on his chin.
mcqs.why: He wishes he had whiskers on his chin, so that he would look big and strong.

mcqs.q: The boy wants that no one would dare to ______ him.
mcqs.why: He wishes to be big so that no one would dare to tease him or take away his toys.

mcqs.q: People take away the boy's:
mcqs.why: The boy wishes to be big so that no one would take away his toys.

mcqs.q: In the model answer, the writer does not like being:
mcqs.why: The model answer says: 'I do not like being shy and speaking in a low voice.'

mcqs.q: The writer of the model answer wants to speak ______ in class.
mcqs.why: The model answer says: 'I want to become brave and speak clearly in class.'

mcqs.q: The poem "I wish..." is recited loudly with:
mcqs.why: The fun exercise says: 'Recite the poem "I wish..." loudly with actions.'

lessons.title: 4.2 Reading - Saifullah and His Peacock Miru
lessons.notes_html:
The Story

Saifullah was a young boy who had a pet peacock named Miru. One night Miru did not come home. Saifullah searched everywhere but could not find him. He was very sad. The word 'night' is used three times in the story.

The next day he learnt that a farmer had shot a peacock. Saifullah ran to the farmer's house. He knew the dead peacock was Miru because he saw his silver ring on the peacock's foot. He began to cry, and the farmer also wept. The farmer said he was sorry and promised that he would never shoot a peacock again.

People in the Story

  • There are three main characters: Saifullah, his father and the farmer.
  • Saifullah speaks three dialogues and the farmer speaks four.
  • "Miru, Miru! Where are you?" - these words are spoken by Saifullah. (The book's printed answer for this line is mixed up; the story shows Saifullah calling for his lost peacock.)

Key Points

  • Miru was Saifullah's pet peacock.
  • Saifullah knew the peacock by the silver ring on its foot.
  • The farmer was sorry and promised never to shoot a peacock again.

mcqs.q: Miru was Saifullah's pet:
mcqs.why: Miru was Saifullah's pet peacock. One night Miru did not come home, and Saifullah searched everywhere for him.

mcqs.q: The word 'night' is used how many times in the story?
mcqs.why: The word 'night' is used three times in the story, as the book's answer counts.

mcqs.q: Who shot the peacock?
mcqs.why: A farmer shot the peacock. Saifullah ran to the farmer's house when he learnt this.

mcqs.q: Saifullah knew the dead peacock was Miru because of:
options: the silver ring on its foot
mcqs.why: He saw his silver ring on the peacock's foot, so he knew the peacock was Miru.

mcqs.q: What did the farmer promise?
options: To never shoot a peacock again
mcqs.why: The farmer said he was sorry and promised that he would never shoot a peacock again.

mcqs.q: How many main characters are there in the story?
mcqs.why: There are three main characters in the story: Saifullah, his father and the farmer.

mcqs.q: Who speaks the most dialogues in the story?
mcqs.why: Saifullah speaks three dialogues, while the farmer speaks four dialogues - the most in the story.

mcqs.q: Who says, "Miru, Miru! Where are you?"
mcqs.why: Saifullah calls out for his lost peacock. The book's printed answer for this line is mixed up; in the story it is Saifullah who searches and calls for Miru.

mcqs.q: Miru did not come home:
mcqs.why: One night Miru did not come home. Saifullah was very sad and searched everywhere.

mcqs.q: When Saifullah saw the dead peacock, he:
mcqs.why: Saifullah began to cry, and seeing him cry, the farmer also wept and said he was sorry.

lessons.title: 4.2 Reading - Word Meanings: Saifullah and Miru
lessons.notes_html:
Word Meanings

  • pet - an animal kept at home (Saifullah's pet peacock Miru)
  • wander - move around without any purpose
  • search - try to find something
  • ploughing - preparing the soil for sowing seeds
  • tearfully - crying
  • sobbing - crying noisily
  • console - comfort someone who is sad

Key Points

  • 'Search' means try to find something.
  • 'Ploughing' is preparing the soil for sowing seeds.
  • 'Console' means comfort someone who is sad.

mcqs.q: 'Pet' means:
mcqs.why: A pet is an animal kept at home, like Saifullah's pet peacock Miru.

mcqs.q: 'Wander' means:
mcqs.why: 'Wander' means move around without any purpose, as the book's meanings list tells us.

mcqs.q: 'Search' means:
mcqs.why: 'Search' means try to find something. Saifullah searched everywhere for Miru.

mcqs.q: 'Ploughing' means:
options: preparing the soil for sowing seeds
mcqs.why: 'Ploughing' means preparing the soil for sowing seeds.

mcqs.why: 'Tearfully' means crying. Saifullah spoke tearfully when he found Miru.

mcqs.why: Saifullah tried to find his lost peacock Miru, so he searched everywhere for him.

mcqs.q: A farmer ploughs his field to:

mcqs.q: If your friend is sad and you comfort him, you ______ him.
mcqs.why: To console means to comfort someone who is sad.

lessons.title: 4.3 Writing - Using Better Words
lessons.notes_html:
Synonyms - Better Words

We can make our writing better by using richer words with the same meaning. These are called synonyms.

  • chosen - selected
  • biggest - largest
  • competitions - tournaments
  • chance - opportunity
  • internationally - throughout the world
  • team - group
  • initial - preliminary
  • also - Additionally
  • participants - contestants
  • first - top
  • got - bagged

Example: Our hockey team got the first position. = Our hockey team bagged the top position.

Key Points

  • 'Chosen' can be written as 'selected'.
  • 'Chance' can be written as 'opportunity'.
  • 'Got' can be written as 'bagged' and 'first' as 'top'.

mcqs.q: 'Chosen' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better word for 'chosen' is 'selected'.

mcqs.q: 'Biggest' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better word for 'biggest' is 'largest'.

mcqs.q: 'Competitions' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better word for 'competitions' is 'tournaments'.

mcqs.q: 'Chance' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better word for 'chance' is 'opportunity'.

mcqs.q: 'Internationally' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better phrase for 'internationally' is 'throughout the world'.

mcqs.q: 'Initial' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better word for 'initial' is 'preliminary'.

mcqs.q: 'Participants' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better word for 'participants' is 'contestants'.

mcqs.q: "Our hockey team got the first position." Using better words:
options: Our hockey team bagged the top position.
Our hockey team selected the large position.
Our hockey team got the top prize.
Our hockey team bagged the first cup.

mcqs.q: 'Team' can be written as:
mcqs.why: The book's better word for 'team' is 'group'.

mcqs.q: Words with the same meaning, used to make writing better, are called:
mcqs.why: Words like chosen/selected and chance/opportunity have the same meaning; such words are called synonyms.

lessons.title: 4.3 Writing - The Beginning, Middle and End of a Story
lessons.notes_html:
Parts of a Story

Every story has three parts: a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning introduces the characters, the middle tells what happens, and the end tells how it finishes.

Model Story

  • Beginning: Ali was a poor farmer. He had a small piece of land. He worked hard but earned very little.
  • Middle: One day, while digging his field, Ali found a pot full of gold coins. He became rich. He bought more land and helped the poor people of his village.
  • End: Ali lived happily with his family. Everyone in the village loved and respected him.

Key Points

  • A story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
  • The beginning introduces the characters.
  • The end tells how the story finishes.

mcqs.q: Every story has ______ main parts.
mcqs.why: Every story has three parts: a beginning, a middle and an end.

mcqs.q: The beginning of a story:
mcqs.why: The beginning introduces the characters; the middle tells what happens and the end tells how it finishes.

mcqs.q: In the model story, Ali was a:
mcqs.why: The model story begins: 'Ali was a poor farmer. He had a small piece of land.'

mcqs.q: Ali found ______ while digging his field.
options: a pot full of gold coins
mcqs.why: In the middle of the story, Ali found a pot full of gold coins while digging his field.

mcqs.q: After becoming rich, Ali:
options: bought more land and helped the poor
mcqs.why: Ali bought more land and helped the poor people of his village.

mcqs.q: The end of the model story tells that Ali:
mcqs.why: The end says: 'Ali lived happily with his family. Everyone in the village loved and respected him.'

mcqs.q: The middle of a story tells:
mcqs.why: The middle tells what happens - in the model story, Ali finds the gold and becomes rich.

mcqs.q: Which part comes FIRST in a story?
mcqs.why: A story starts with the beginning, then comes the middle, and then the end.

mcqs.q: Finding the gold coins is part of the ______ of the model story.
mcqs.why: Finding the pot of gold coins is the main event, so it belongs to the middle of the story.

mcqs.q: "Everyone loved and respected him" belongs to the ______ of the story.
mcqs.why: This line tells how the story finishes, so it belongs to the end of the story.

lessons.title: 4.4 Grammar - Possessive Adjectives
lessons.notes_html:
Possessive Adjectives

Possessive adjectives show who owns something: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.

The Jumbled Sentences (Corrected)

  • His house is very big.
  • Our teacher checks our homework daily.
  • Their house is near the school.
  • Your bag is heavy.
  • I brush my teeth daily.
  • She is washing her clothes.
  • The peacock spreads its feathers.

Key Points

  • Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.
  • We use 'its' for animals and things.
  • 'Their' is used for more than one person.

mcqs.q: ______ house is very big. (for a man)
mcqs.why: For a man or boy we use 'his': 'His house is very big.'

mcqs.q: ______ teacher checks our homework daily. (for we)
mcqs.why: For 'we' we use 'our': 'Our teacher checks our homework daily.'

mcqs.q: The peacock spreads ______ feathers.
mcqs.why: For animals and things we use 'its': 'The peacock spreads its feathers.'

mcqs.q: She is washing ______ clothes.
mcqs.why: For a woman or girl we use 'her': 'She is washing her clothes.'

mcqs.q: I brush ______ teeth daily.
mcqs.why: For 'I' we use 'my': 'I brush my teeth daily.'

mcqs.q: ______ bag is heavy. (speaking to you)
mcqs.why: For 'you' we use 'your': 'Your bag is heavy.'

mcqs.q: ______ house is near the school. (for they)
mcqs.why: For 'they' we use 'their': 'Their house is near the school.'

mcqs.q: Which of these is a possessive adjective?
mcqs.why: Possessive adjectives are my, your, his, her, its, our and their. 'Their' shows ownership.

mcqs.q: Possessive adjectives show:
mcqs.why: Possessive adjectives show who owns something, like 'my teeth' and 'her clothes'.

mcqs.q: The cat is drinking ______ milk.
mcqs.why: For animals we use 'its': the cat drinks its milk, just like the peacock spreads its feathers.

lessons.title: 4.4 Grammar - Used To
lessons.notes_html:
What 'Used To' Means

We use 'used to' for things we did in the past but do not do now.

My Grandmother

  • When my grandmother was young, she used to be very naughty.
  • She used to climb trees.
  • She used to waste a lot of water.

More Examples from the Book

  • When I was in Class One, I used to collect feathers of different birds.
  • My grandfather used to walk to school because there were no buses in those days.
  • My grandmother used to wear colourful dresses.

Key Points

  • 'Used to' shows a past habit that has stopped.
  • Grandmother used to climb trees when she was young.
  • Grandfather used to walk to school.

mcqs.q: We use 'used to' for things we did:
options: in the past but do not do now
mcqs.why: 'Used to' is for past habits that have stopped, like climbing trees in childhood.

mcqs.q: When my grandmother was young, she used to be very:
mcqs.why: The book's answer says: 'When my grandmother was young, she used to be very naughty.'

mcqs.q: Grandmother used to ______ trees.
mcqs.why: The book's answer is: 'She used to climb trees.'

mcqs.q: Grandmother used to waste a lot of:
mcqs.why: The book's answer is: 'She used to waste a lot of water.'

mcqs.q: When I was in Class One, I used to collect:
mcqs.why: The book's example says: 'When I was in Class One, I used to collect feathers of different birds.'

mcqs.q: My grandfather used to ______ to school.
mcqs.why: My grandfather used to walk to school because there were no buses in those days.

mcqs.q: Grandmother used to wear ______ dresses.
mcqs.why: The book's example says: 'My grandmother used to wear colourful dresses.'

mcqs.q: Which sentence shows a past habit with 'used to'?
mcqs.why: 'She used to climb trees' shows a past habit. The other sentences are present or future.

mcqs.q: "There were no buses in those days" explains why grandfather:
mcqs.why: Grandfather used to walk to school because there were no buses in those days.

mcqs.q: 'Used to' is followed by the ______ form of the verb.
mcqs.why: After 'used to' we use the base form: used to climb, used to walk, used to collect, used to wear.

lessons.title: 4.4 Grammar - Do and Have: Main Verbs and Helping Verbs
lessons.notes_html:
Main Verbs and Helping Verbs

'Do' and 'have' can be main verbs (they show the main action) or helping verbs (they help another verb).

  • Do your work. - main verb
  • Do you like mangoes? - helping verb
  • I have two brothers. - main verb
  • I have finished my work. - helping verb
  • We do our homework daily. - main verb; Do you speak English? - helping verb.

Do/Does and Have/Has

  • With he, she, it: does and has. (He does his work; She has a doll.)
  • With I, we, you, they: do and have. (They do their work; We have a car.)

Key Points

  • 'Do' and 'have' can be main verbs or helping verbs.
  • Use 'does' and 'has' with he, she and it.
  • Use 'do' and 'have' with I, we, you and they.

mcqs.why: In 'Do your work', 'do' shows the main action, so it is a main verb (M in the book's key).

mcqs.q: In "Do you like mangoes?", 'do' is a:
mcqs.why: Here 'do' only helps the main verb 'like' to make a question, so it is a helping verb (H in the book's key).

mcqs.q: In "I have two brothers", 'have' is a:
mcqs.why: Here 'have' shows possession as the main action, so it is a main verb (M in the book's key).

mcqs.q: In "I have finished my work", 'have' is a:
mcqs.why: Here 'have' helps the main verb 'finished', so it is a helping verb (H in the book's key).

mcqs.why: With 'he, she, it' we use 'does': He does his work daily.

mcqs.q: She ______ a new doll.
mcqs.why: With 'he, she, it' we use 'has': She has a new doll.

mcqs.q: They ______ their work daily.
mcqs.why: With 'I, we, you, they' we use 'do': They do their work daily.

mcqs.q: We ______ a big car.
mcqs.why: With 'we' we use 'have': We have a big car.

mcqs.why: A helping verb helps another verb, like 'do' in 'Do you speak English?' and 'have' in 'I have finished my work.'

mcqs.why: 'Do' shows the main action (doing homework), so it is a main verb here.

lessons.title: 4.4 Grammar - Degrees of Adjectives
lessons.notes_html:
The Three Degrees

Adjectives have three degrees: positive (tall), comparative (taller) and superlative (tallest).

The Table

  • tall - taller - tallest
  • clean - cleaner - cleanest
  • pretty - prettier - prettiest
  • small - smaller - smallest
  • slow - slower - slowest
  • dirty - dirtier - dirtiest
  • sweet - sweeter - sweetest
  • fast - faster - fastest
  • tasty - tastier - tastiest
  • short - shorter - shortest

Rule: when an adjective ends in 'y', change 'y' to 'i' before adding -er and -est: pretty - prettier - prettiest.

Key Points

  • Comparative = adjective + -er; superlative = adjective + -est.
  • Pretty becomes prettier and prettiest.
  • Dirty becomes dirtier and dirtiest.

mcqs.why: Dirty - dirtier - dirtiest. The 'y' changes to 'i' before -est.

mcqs.why: Tall - taller - tallest. We add -er for the comparative degree.

mcqs.why: Fast - faster - fastest. We add -est for the superlative degree.

mcqs.why: Tasty - tastier - tastiest. The 'y' changes to 'i' before -er.

mcqs.why: Sweet - sweeter - sweetest. We add -est for the superlative.

mcqs.why: Clean - cleaner - cleanest. We add -er to 'clean' for the comparative degree.

mcqs.why: Adjectives have three degrees: positive (tall), comparative (taller) and superlative (tallest).

mcqs.why: Small - smaller - smallest. We add -est to 'small' for the superlative degree.

mcqs.why: We change 'y' to 'i': pretty - prettier, dirty - dirtier, tasty - tastier.

lessons.title: 4.4 Grammar - Choosing with 'Or'
lessons.notes_html:
Asking About Choices

We use 'or' in questions to ask about a choice between two things.

Model Questions and Answers

  • Does Umer eat a mango or an apple in breakfast? - Umer eats a mango in breakfast.
  • Does Samad eat a banana or an apple after lunch? - Samad eats an apple after lunch.
  • Do you listen to pop music or folk music? - I listen to folk music.
  • Does Hira listen to pop music or sufi music? - Hira listens to sufi music.

Notice: in the answers, 'or' and the thing not chosen are dropped.

Key Points

  • 'Or' joins two choices in a question.
  • Umer eats a mango; Samad eats an apple.
  • The answer keeps only the chosen thing.

mcqs.why: The model answer is: 'Hira listens to sufi music.'

lessons.title: 4.5 Study Skills - Words from 'Farmyard'
lessons.notes_html:
Words in Alphabetical Order

The words farm, fry, arm, yard, ram, mad and far, put in alphabetical order, are: arm, far, farm, fry, mad, ram, yard.

Words from 'Farmyard'

Words that can be made from 'Farmyard' are: farmyard, farm, fry, arm, yard, ram, mad, far, army, ray, day, may, yam, radar, drama, marry, armada.

Model sentences: We live on a farm. We fry fish on Fridays. My arm is strong.

Key Points

  • 'Arm' comes first and 'yard' comes last in alphabetical order.
  • 'Radar' can be made from 'Farmyard' - it uses only its letters.
  • 'Drama' and 'armada' are longer words from 'Farmyard'.

mcqs.why: The order is: arm, far, farm, fry, mad, ram, yard. 'Arm' begins with 'a' and comes first.

mcqs.why: 'Farmer' needs the letter 'e', which is not in 'Farmyard'. Drama, army and armada use only its letters.

mcqs.why: The model sentence is: 'We fry fish on Fridays.'

mcqs.why: The order is: arm, far, farm, fry... 'Far' is shorter than 'farm', so it comes just before 'farm'.

mcqs.why: The list is: arm, far, farm, fry, mad, ram, yard. 'Mad' is in it.

mcqs.why: The model sentence is: 'My arm is strong.'

mcqs.why: 'Armada' is one of the longer words the book makes from 'Farmyard', along with drama and marry.

mcqs.why: The model sentence is: 'We live on a farm.'

lessons.title: 5.2 Reading - Floods: A Blessing in Disguise
lessons.notes_html:
About the Text

The 2010 monsoon floods were a disaster, but for some people they proved to be a blessing in disguise. Four people tell how the floods changed their lives.

The Four People

  • Haseena Mai: a poor widow who worked as a maid. An NGO gave her 50 hens and their feed for three months. Now she has her own poultry farm and earns about Rs 30,000 a month. She has become an inspiration for many women.
  • Rana Mumtaz Ali: his land had become barren because of salinity. After the floods, about 100 acres became fertile again. He got 1,760 kg of wheat per acre, and the crop was so thick that even a snake could not find a place in it.
  • Muhammad Sharif: around 15 kilometres of his infertile land became cultivable. His wheat production rose from 2,200 kg to 2,600 kg per acre.
  • Jamshed: he has a lake where he catches up to 15 kg of fish. After the floods, fisheries production increased by about 30 percent.

Key Points

  • Haseena Mai got 50 hens and now earns about Rs 30,000 a month.
  • Rana Mumtaz Ali's 100 acres became fertile again.
  • Fisheries production increased by about 30 percent after the floods.

mcqs.why: The text tells how the 2010 monsoon floods proved to be a blessing in disguise for four people.

mcqs.why: Haseena Mai is a poor widow who worked as a maid before the NGO helped her.

mcqs.why: The text says she now earns about Rs 30,000 a month from her poultry farm.

mcqs.why: His land became barren because of salinity, and after the floods about 100 acres became fertile again.

mcqs.why: About 100 acres of his land became fertile again after the floods.

mcqs.why: He got 1,760 kg of wheat per acre, and the crop was so thick that even a snake could not find a place in it.

mcqs.why: His wheat production increased from 2,200 kg per acre to 2,600 kg per acre after the floods.

mcqs.why: Jamshed has a lake where he catches up to 15 kg of fish.

mcqs.why: The text says fisheries production increased by about 30 percent after the floods.

lessons.title: 5.2 Reading - Word Meanings in the Floods Text
lessons.notes_html:
Word Meanings

  • cattle - animals like cows and buffaloes (given in the book)
  • blessing - something that is good for you
  • disguise - something that hides the true appearance
  • widow - a woman whose husband has died
  • maid - a female servant
  • feed - food for animals

  • disaster - something that causes great damage

  • salinity - the quality of containing salt
  • fertile - land on which crops grow well
  • cultivated - used for growing crops

Key Points

  • 'Barren' land cannot grow crops; 'fertile' land grows crops well.
  • 'Receded' means moved back - the flood water moved back.
  • 'Livelihood' means a way of earning money to live on.

lessons.title: 5.2 Reading - Making Questions about the Floods Text
lessons.notes_html:
Making Questions from Given Answers

Read the answer and make a question for it. The underlined words in the answer tell us what to ask about.

  • Answer: Haseena Mai received 50 hens. - Question: How many hens did Haseena Mai receive?
  • Answer: The flood water receded in October. - Question: When did the flood water recede?
  • Answer: Rana Mumtaz Ali's land became fertile. - Question: Whose land became fertile after the floods?
  • Answer: Jamshed catches fish in the lake. - Question: Where does Jamshed catch fish?
  • Answer: The land became barren because of salinity. - Question: Why did the land become barren?

Asking the Right Question Word

  • Number: How many | Time: When | Person: Who / Whose | Place: Where | Reason: Why

Key Points

  • Ask 'How many' for numbers and 'When' for time.
  • Ask 'Whose' for the owner and 'Why' for a reason.
  • The underlined words in the answer show what to ask about.

mcqs.q: Answer: "Haseena Mai received 50 hens." The best question is:
options: How many hens did Haseena Mai receive?
mcqs.why: The underlined words are '50 hens', a number, so we ask: 'How many hens did Haseena Mai receive?'

mcqs.q: Answer: "The flood water receded in October." The best question is:
options: When did the flood water recede?
mcqs.why: The underlined words tell the time (in October), so we ask: 'When did the flood water recede?'

mcqs.q: Answer: "Rana Mumtaz Ali's land became fertile." The best question is:
options: Whose land became fertile after the floods?
mcqs.why: The underlined name shows the owner, so we ask: 'Whose land became fertile after the floods?'

mcqs.why: The underlined words 'in the lake' tell the place, so we ask: 'Where does Jamshed catch fish?'

mcqs.q: Answer: "The land became barren because of salinity." The best question is:
options: Why did the land become barren?
mcqs.why: The underlined words give a reason (because of salinity), so we ask: 'Why did the land become barren?'

mcqs.why: We ask 'How many' for numbers, like 'How many hens did Haseena Mai receive?'

mcqs.q: To ask about a reason, we use:
mcqs.why: We ask 'Why' for a reason, like 'Why did the land become barren?' - 'Because of salinity.'

mcqs.why: We ask 'Whose' for the owner: 'Whose land became fertile?' - 'Rana Mumtaz Ali's land.'

mcqs.q: Answer: "Haseena Mai earns Rs 30,000 a month." A good question is:
options: How much does Haseena Mai earn in a month?
mcqs.why: The answer tells an amount of money, so we ask: 'How much does Haseena Mai earn in a month?'

options: How much fish does Jamshed catch?
mcqs.why: The answer tells a quantity (15 kg), so we ask: 'How much fish does Jamshed catch?'

lessons.title: 5.4 Grammar - Pronouns: Kaleem and His Family

lessons.title: 5.4 Grammar - Degrees of Adjectives: Special Forms
lessons.notes_html:
Special Forms

Some adjectives do not take -er and -est. They have special forms:

  • good - better - best
  • bad - worse - worst
  • early - earlier - earliest
  • many - more - most
  • little - lesser - least
  • useful - more useful - most useful
  • happy - happier - happiest
  • beautiful - more beautiful - most beautiful

Long adjectives like useful and beautiful take 'more' and 'most' instead of -er and -est.

Key Points

  • Good - better - best; bad - worse - worst.
  • Many - more - most; little - lesser - least.
  • Long adjectives use more and most.

lessons.title: 5.4 Grammar - The Superlative Degree
lessons.notes_html:
The Table

  • Arif: 62 kg, 4 feet 8 inches, 509 marks, 143 runs
  • Bachal: 79 kg, 4 feet 4 inches, 583 marks, 109 runs
  • Latif: 74 kg, 4 feet 9 inches, 533 marks, 179 runs
  • Nasir: 69 kg, 4 feet 2 inches, 574 marks, 184 runs
  • Peer Bakhsh: 63 kg, 4 feet 5 inches, 594 marks, 112 runs

Superlative Sentences

  • Bachal is the heaviest of all the boys.
  • Peer Bakhsh has got the highest marks in the class.
  • Bachal has made the least runs in cricket.
  • Nasir is the shortest of all the boys.
  • Arif has got the lowest marks in the class.
  • Nasir has made the most runs in cricket.
  • Latif is the tallest of all the boys.
  • Arif is the lightest of all the boys.

We use 'the' before superlative adjectives: the tallest, the heaviest.

Key Points

  • Bachal is the heaviest; Arif is the lightest.
  • Peer Bakhsh has the highest marks; Arif has the lowest.
  • Nasir made the most runs; Bachal made the least.

lessons.title: 5.4 Grammar - Giving Reasons with 'Because'
lessons.notes_html:
Using 'Because'

We use 'because' to give a reason. It joins two parts of a sentence: what happened, and why it happened.

Sentences from the Book

  • We got late because there was a traffic jam.
  • My friend did not come to school because he was sick.
  • Our teacher is happy because we have done our work.
  • The old man carries a white stick because he cannot see.
  • Salim did not do his homework because he wanted to play.
  • Razia and Hameed washed the dishes because their mother was sick.
  • Our cricket team is practising hard because they want to win the match.

Model Reasons

  • I cannot use my old bag because it is torn.
  • My friend was absent because he was ill.
  • I get up early because I do not want to miss the school bus.
  • He could not run because he had hurt his foot.
  • I do not play today because I am not feeling well.
  • We should finish our homework on time because the teacher checks it daily.

Key Points

  • 'Because' gives the reason for something.
  • The old man carries a white stick because he cannot see.
  • Razia and Hameed washed the dishes because their mother was sick.

lessons.title: 5.5 Study Skills - Words from 'University'
lessons.notes_html:
Words in Alphabetical Order

Words like sun, very, run, nest, unity and suit, in alphabetical order, begin with 'in' and end with words like vine, yet and yes. In the list, 'suit' comes just before 'sun' because 'i' comes before 'n'.

Words from 'University'

Many words can be made from 'University', for example: sun, very, run, nest, unity, suit, in, vine, yet, yes, rust, true, tune, turn, unit, vein, rest, sent, nuts, tiny, rite, tier, site, user, rise, vein.

Model Sentences

  • The sun is shining brightly.
  • Unity is our strength.
  • The bird made a nest in the tree.

Key Points

  • 'Suit' comes just before 'sun' in alphabetical order.
  • The model sentence says: 'Unity is our strength.'
  • Many small words can be made from 'University'.

mcqs.q: In the book's alphabetical list of 'University' words, which word comes first?
mcqs.why: The book's alphabetical list begins with 'in', because words beginning with 'i' come before 'n', 'r' and 's' words.

mcqs.q: In alphabetical order, 'suit' comes just before:
mcqs.why: Both begin with 'su', but 'suit' has 'i' next and 'sun' has 'n'; 'i' comes before 'n', so 'suit' comes just before 'sun'.

mcqs.q: The model sentence about the sun says: "The sun is ______ brightly."
mcqs.why: The model sentence is: 'The sun is shining brightly.'

mcqs.q: The model sentence says: "______ is our strength."
mcqs.why: The model sentence is: 'Unity is our strength.' 'Unity' can be made from the letters of 'University'.

mcqs.q: The bird made a ______ in the tree. (model sentence)
mcqs.why: The model sentence is: 'The bird made a nest in the tree.'

mcqs.q: Which word can be made from the letters of 'University'?
mcqs.why: 'Nest' uses only letters of 'University' (n, e, s, t). Pencil needs 'p' and 'l', which are not in 'University'.

mcqs.q: Which word can NOT be made from 'University'?
mcqs.why: 'Plant' needs 'p' and 'l', which are not in 'University'. Vine, true and rust use only its letters.

mcqs.q: In alphabetical order, which comes first: sun, run, very?
mcqs.why: 'Run' begins with 'r', which comes before 's' (sun) and 'v' (very), so 'run' comes first of these.

mcqs.q: Which of these 'University' words names something a bird makes?
mcqs.why: A bird makes a nest. The model sentence is: 'The bird made a nest in the tree.'

mcqs.q: 'Unity' means:
mcqs.why: Unity means being together as one, which is why the model sentence says: 'Unity is our strength.'

lessons.title: 5.6 Fun - Our National Flag and Words from 'Hospital'
lessons.notes_html:
Our National Flag (Poem by Zunaira H. Gwadri)

  • The white colour in our flag shows the minorities of our country.
  • The green colour shows peace and prosperity.
  • The crescent shows Islamic grace.
  • The star shows spiritual progress.

Pictures and Words from 'Hospital'

  • In the first picture, a caterpillar is going up in a hot-air balloon.
  • In the second picture, a bird is looking at the caterpillar.
  • In the third picture, a grasshopper is talking to the caterpillar.

Words from 'Hospital' include: hospital, host, post, soap, ship, shop, stop, top, pot, hot, hat, pat, tap, pit, sit, hit, hip, hop, ash, has, also, lost, last, past, tail, sail, salt, slip, slot, pilot, pistol, postal. The word 'plate' can NOT be made because 'Hospital' has no letter 'e'.

Model sentences: We should wash our hands with soap. The ship sails on the sea.

Key Points

  • White shows minorities; green shows peace and prosperity.
  • The crescent shows Islamic grace and the star shows spiritual progress.
  • 'Plate' cannot be made from 'Hospital' - there is no 'e'.
